claims.paraphrased_claim: Iron deficiency is supported by low ferritin, increased iron-binding capacity and reduced transferrin saturation; low ferritin is particularly specific for iron deficiency outside major confounding contexts.
Low serum iron is not specific for iron deficiency because it can also occur in chronic inflammatory disease.
Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and can be elevated in inflammatory states, so an apparently normal ferritin does not automatically exclude coexisting iron deficiency.

Anemia of chronic disease/inflammation is considered in patients with chronic inflammatory illness and microcytic or normocytic anemia; iron studies typically require interpretation of ferritin, transferrin/iron-binding measures and reticulocyte context together.
In inflammatory states, iron deficiency can coexist with anemia of inflammation, and intermediate ferritin results may require additional markers or context rather than a single definitive label.
